Why cryin’ and not crying?

Will: I really like Thursdays on Thursday.

Why can't they all ... be from California — No! I mean why can't all the phrases found in crossword puzzles be lovely familiar phrases that fit in this puzzle like a favorite slipper on my foot — but then my appreciation of the puzzle comes crashing down upon realizing that I had no chance of Eidentifying a Billie Eilish tune, no less anything about Ms. Eilish. Oh, well. But I sure enjoyed the phrases!

FORCRYINOUTLOUD, what does it take to get a tricky Thursday around here.  

I did have to smile though because my wife and I just decided tonight to make the French 75 the signature cocktail at our Thanksgiving dinner, so GIN was a gimme.

I really liked this. Not really a Thursday theme, but I thought it was a reasonably challenging grid so perhaps Thursday is appropriate. And four 15 letter entries is very elegant.

Raise your hand if you thought the “doc that prevents leaks” ought to be URO(logist). What a great clue for NDA. I think there were a lot of decent clues for common fill that I didn’t get right away.

DOECHII—I thought I had at least heard of all the famous rappers from these puzzles but I guess it’s like Native American tribes there’s always more. I had no idea how to parse this: DO ECHII? DOE CHII? DOECH II? Turns out it’s all one word.

WINK? PING? DING? Ok TING the last thing I would have thought of.

Yeah we’ll give some constructor’s license for no G in CRYIN. No use cryin’ over spilt milk.

I could nit a few other clues but honestly I like being stumped on Thursday and if takes a stretchy clue to help then bring it on! I’m A FAN today.
I enjoyed it, even though actually, time isn’t really a scalar.  It is a component of a 4-vector.  Good enough for a crossword puzzle though.
When the trick is...there's no trick?
Thank goodness for crosses or I never would have gotten DOECHII. Fun puzzle.

A comment on the column, not the puzzle: You need to review your physics lessons. If a value is a SCALAR quantity, it has magnitude only. If it has magnitude and direction, it is a vector quantity. Examples would be speed (rate of travel) is a scalar, while velocity (rate of travel toward a target) is a vector. Mass (amount of material present) is scalar, while weight (force due to gravity on the amount of material present) is a vector.

So, TING has practically always been given a definitional clue.  It’s never been clued before with something as intriguing as [Your attention please!].  SKY has appeared almost 450 times in the major crossword outlets, but never clued anything close to [View from a hammock].

Nor have we seen, in all the years of crosswords, in all the outlets, anything like the marvelous [Doc that prevents leaks] for NDA, and [Remedies for the broken hearted?] for STENTS.

James Mattina has a unique way of looking at things.  And humor.  These things elevate a puzzle, make it entertain and pop out. 

And originality.  Such as taking uber-engaging idioms that start with FOR, and cluing them literally.  That is fun personified.

All I can say, James, is that I’m glad you and crosswords have crossed paths.  More please.  This puzzle was a hoot and a day-lifter.  Thank you for making it!

For all those who question whether Alex, of *A Clockwork Orange*, can be considered a protagonist, it is worth remembering that, in the original version of Burgess's novel, Alex, now eighteen, meets up with one of his former Droogs, Pete, who has married and settled down. This encounter convinces Alex himself, to give up his ultra-violence, and perhaps start a family himself. This chapter was omitted from the first *American* editions (and Kubrick's movie), by editors who felt that American audiences would prefer a darker ending. (My edition includes that chapter, but set in different typography--weird.) Does this make Alex any more of a protagonist? Probably not. But it doesn't make him less-- --I gotta work this in, for @Grant, if no one else: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=px2bhEOq6O4&list=RDpx2bhEOq6O4&start_radio=1 IYKYK

It's simpler than that.  Most of those questioning this point don't realize that a protagonist is simply the main character (or one of the main characters) who moves the plot forward, and about whose actions, thoughts, etc., the story is centered.  There can be multiple protagonists, who may be, but are not necessarily, heroic.  The word is based on Greek elements meaning first (i.e. main) actor.

An antagonist is the one who opposes the protagonist, usually having opposite interests.  So in many superhero movies that center on a villain, that villain can be said to be the protagonist, while the crimefighter is the antagonist, provided that the story is told from the villain's point of view.
